title: Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline
abstract: Back to Articles Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline Enterprise + Article Published October 16, 2026 Upvote 9 +3 Will Jennings WillJenningsDC Follow nvidia Kiran Praveen kipraveen Follow nvidia Sriharsha Niverty sniverty Follow nvidia Raviraj Joshi ravirajoshi Follow nvidia Markus Kliegl mkliegl-nv Follow nvidia Yev Meyer nv-3mei Follow nvidia Utkarsh Vaidya uvaidya Follow nvidia Niket Agarwal niketagarwal Follow nvidia Native-script data for 22 languages, romanized data for twelve, and a reusable GPU-accelerated pipeline for translation, quality assessment, and repair. Authors: AI4Bharat — Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan, Mitesh Khapra, Anoop Kunchukuttan. NVIDIA — Niket Agarwal, Raviraj Joshi, Anusha Kamath, Markus Kliegl, Yev Meyer, Sriharsha Niverty, Kiran Praveen, Utkarsh Vaidya. We're excited to introduce Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 approximately 2.8 trillion tokens across 22 Indian languages , releasing soon alongside the open, GPU-accelerated data generation pipeline used to create it. These are the 22 languages listed in India's Constitution: the first languages for 97% of Indians, or nearly 1.2 billion citizens at the 2011 Census. Developed by NVIDIA with IIT Madras , India's premier engineering institute, and its AI4Bharat lab, this release gives model builders a substantial new resource for Indic pretraining. The pipeline captures the full generation recipe, including prompts, LLM workflows, and quality checks, so developers can adapt it to their own source material and generate more data for their needs. AI4Bharat, IIT Madras' Indian language research lab, builds open-source datasets and models for Indian languages. Its resources, such as Sangraha , an open pretraining corpus for 22 Indian languages, have helped lay the foundation for open Indic language-model research. Our joint open-source release represents a substantial expansion of the open synthetic Indic training data that will be available to the community. It brings a broad mix of curated English material, including mathematics, code, and question-answer content, into Indian languages, giving teams more training material for building models that can explain technical concepts, work through problems, and answer questions in those languages. Every record traces back to a curated source document, and each output is checked against its input, so the synthetic text stays grounded in real information. Mitesh Khapra, who heads AI4Bharat and made the 2025 TIME100 AI list , has named the core problem: Indian language technology trails English because "we do not have enough data for Indian languages." We're answering that call with more data, plus an open recipe for generating more. The corpus also accounts for how people write. It includes native-script data for all 22 languages and romanized text for twelve, spanning 34 language-script configurations. Our workflows combine document-level translation, quality assessment, and targeted repair, with checks to preserve content such as equations, tables, and code. This data complements naturally authored Indic text, which remains essential for local knowledge and cultural context. We're sharing the open generation recipe so the community can not just reproduce the data but take this work further. Teams can use the corpus directly, adapt the prompts and quality checks, or bring their own source documents to the workflow. By opening up both the data and the process, we aim to make large-scale Indic data generation more accessible and enable more developers to contribute to stronger models across Indian languages. Continued pretraining for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL added 10 billion Indic tokens, drawn from a twelve-language subset of this corpus and natural Indic text. Our technical report on the model covers the full story. We plan to build on this corpus in future Nemotron models. What is in the corpus? Figure 1. The corpus contains 2,601.0 billion native-script tokens and 224.6 billion romanized tokens. Counts use the Gemma-4 tokenizer. Document records include translations and script variants of shared sources; they are not counts of unique English documents. The corpus has two groups of language configurations: Native-script and romanized data: Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu. Native-script data: Assamese, Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Manipuri, Sanskrit, Santali, and Sindhi. Here, native-script describes the writing system: the text is still translated from English. Romanized means Indic-language text written in Latin script, not an English translation. For each of the twelve dual-script languages, romanization covers a subset of the accepted native-script translations. This distinction matters when constructing a training mixture. Native and romanized records offer different script exposure, but can express the same underlying content. The token counts describe the retained corpus, including accepted rewrites, rather than a training run's token budget. Counts also depend on the tokenizer used, so corpus inventory and training-token counts should be read separately. From English source documents to Indic training data To build this corpus, we start with documents from 15 Nemotron-CC-v2 subsets, covering web text, question-answer material, mathematics, code, and other specialized content. We use NeMo Data Designer , NVIDIA's open-source framework for generating synthetic data, to run translation, quality checks, and targeted repair. Throughout the workflow, we retain each source identifier so developers can trace an output back to its original document. Clear provenance like this is part of what makes open data practical to audit and build on. Figure 2 shows the workflow for twelve languages. Figure 2. Four-stage Indic synthetic-data pipeline for twelve languages, implemented using NeMo Data Designer and Gemma-4-31B-it. We translate English documents, assess translation quality, repair low-scoring outputs, and convert a subset of accepted translations into Latin script. The other ten languages use the separate Indic Translate workflow described below. The twelve-language workflow For these twelve languages, we translate documents in full so the model can use context across paragraphs, tables, and equations. We selected Gemma-4-31B-it by comparing models on complete documents, checking translation quality and preservation of technical content. Our prompts distinguish prose to translate from content to preserve, including code, equations, URLs, and formatting. After translation, we use the same model to assess each output against its English source. A rubric inspired by Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM), an open framework for classifying translation errors by type and severity, covers meaning, fluency, terminology, style, and formatting. We retain only outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 (a rubric score, not an accuracy percentage). For lower-scoring outputs, we use the assessment feedback to guide repairs, then reassess them against the same threshold. This process recovered 438.4 billion tokens across native-script and romanized data, already included in the corpus total. Sampled human reviews and tests with deliberately introduced errors helped identify omissions and residual English, informing improvements to our prompts and checks. Accepted native-script translations also provide the starting point for romanized data. We convert a subset into Latin script and check each result against its native-script input. This separates translation from script conversion. In our initial human comparison, this two-step approach produced fewer hallucinated additions and less residual English than generating romanized text directly from English. The ten-language workflow For the other ten languages, we adapt the workflow to address long-document quality and script-stability issues observed in our comparisons.

title: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale
abstract: Back to Articles Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale Published October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 11 +5 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB.

title: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint
abstract: Back to Articles Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint Enterprise Article Published October 15, 2026 Upvote 44 +38 Kate Soule katesoule Follow ibm-granite Subhajit Chaudhury subhajit1412 Follow ibm-granite Hendrik Strobelt hen Follow ibm-granite Luis A Lastras GrizleeBer Follow ibm-granite Introduced last spring, the Granite Switch project enables a modular approach to model development. Now Granite Switch 4.1 models, armed with a Decision adapter and the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR leaderboard, can move efficiently between natural-language responses, general and specialized decisions, and speech-to-text tasks—all from one hosted endpoint. Specifically, Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B models are configured to include: A new Decision aLoRA for general-purpose decision-making (e.g. v1/systemone), A specialized Guardian aLoRA that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft-Decision-1, GPT-Luna-Decisions, and Clef-Flash on safety-related decision tasks, and Granite-Speech-5.0-Turbo-CTC , the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR Leaderboard , embedded for use in transcription tasks. All three of these technologies (along with the underlying base model) are composed into one model, taking up approximately the same amount of VRAM on a GPU as the base model would by itself. That means more capabilities with fewer GPUs. And because the Switch adapters were built as cache-efficient Activated LoRAs , the KV cache created from a base model generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter-based decisions. Combined with our team's recent vLLM contributions to speed up low rank adapter inferencing, as well as a co-located ASR encoder, Granite Switch 4.1 models can switch between a chat request and a decision request and a spoken request, with blazing fast speeds. Check out our Speech-to-Decisions HF space where granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribes audio, generates summaries, screens for harmful content, and tests 15 other user-defined flags—all running on a single endpoint in real time. Granite Libraries: The OG Decision Models Decision models aren’t new. Our previous release of Granite Libraries features a repository of specialized “decision model” adapters and other specialized task adapters that can be composed into custom Granite Switch models. And while Jev and other closed decision models focus on generality, we’ve found that many of our specialized granitelib adapters can outperform generalists on specialized classification tasks. Compare granitelib adapters with generalist decision models when evaluated on specialized classification tasks. Because adapters share the base model's KV cache, adding specialists alongside a generalist decision adapter costs almost nothing. You get broad coverage from the generalist and higher accuracy from specialists on the tasks you care about. In a “Race” between Granite-Switch-4.1-30B (frozen base Granite + 4 specialized aLoRAs) and Jev-27B (frozen base Qwen model + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite-Switch-4.1-30B was able to complete a real world, 5-step RAG workflow much faster than its competitor. Compose and Extend Your Own Granite Switch Model Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B are released with “batteries included”. They are Granite Switch models that we compiled with a predefined set of helpful adapters. But you don’t need to use our version. Anyone can compose their own Granite Switch model , mixing and matching adapters from Granite Libraries to best meet their needs. Moving forward, we see tremendous opportunity for the community to compose and extend Granite Switch models with custom and third party adapters. We plan to release an Adapter SDK for training adapters in Mellea , along side other tutorials and Granite Switch support. These adapters could be specialized classification adapters to augment decision-based workflows or adapters for specialized language tasks. You could even use custom adapters to teach a 3B parameter version of Granite to play the classic game Doom. Similarly to Jev, our custom 3B parameter Granite Switch model made split second decisions to navigate the Doom game, but was able to do so at 60 - 100 decisions / second, compared to Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second. 1 Unlike Jev, this Granite Switch model can also narrate and respond to your questions while it is playing. We look forward to releasing more details and data on Granite Switch in the upcoming weeks, but until then, we encourage you to try out our latest Switch models and these other helpful resources for getting started. Accessible from anywhere Coming in 8b and 30b sizes, Granite Switch 4.1 can fit wherever your workload runs. The model runs in vllm with a plug-in (see Granite Switch repo below), and has native inference support in llama.cpp and downstream platforms which allows the model to seamlessly swap in for /v1/systemone API calls anywhere they're used, while also servicing traditional chat calls, all with a shared prefix cache. title: Liquid AI Releases d1-ultra: A Multimodal Decision Model That Scores 65 on the AA Decision Index
abstract: Liquid AI has released d1-ultra , its most capable decision model to date. The Liquid AI d1-ultra decision model reads text, images, or both. It answers typed questions with a probability for each possible answer. It does this in one forward pass and generates no output tokens. For developers, that means classification, routing and scoring calls without paying for generated text. It is available now on the Liquid API at $0.042 per million input tokens. A decision model answers bounded questions with probabilities instead of free text. Liquid’s decision model docs describe 3 question types: The docs recommend decision models for routing, moderation, guardrails, triage and LLM-as-judge replacement. They recommend a language model for summarization, chat and code generation. Each request carries a state (the context), optional images , and 1 or more typed questions . The model evaluates every question against the same input in 1 call. The d1 API reference shows responses with output_tokens always at 0. Liquid AI team states that d1-ultra uses a larger open-weight backbone than d1 , along with heavy Liquid-specific customizations. Combined with Liquid’s decision training pipeline, the gains are largest on knowledge tasks. Liquid AI team built d1-ultra for messy cases. Its examples include spotting a circuit board defect against a spec. Another is checking a damage claim against the customer’s photo. Liquid AI compared d1-ultra against its earlier d1 and TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 across 112 evaluations. According to Liquid AI’s announcement , d1-ultra outperforms Jev 1.14 across all tasks at the same price. On the independent Artificial Analysis Decision Index , Liquid reports d1-ultra ranks #1 with a score of 65. The index averages 4 evaluations at 25% each: For context, Artificial Analysis’s Oct 13 launch article listed Jev 1.13 first at 58. GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 followed at 54 each. d1-ultra runs on the Liquid API through the /decisions/v1/systemone endpoint with "model": "d1-ultra" . Liquid says Vercel AI Gateway and OpenRouter support is coming soon. You can test it first in the d1 Playground . Billing covers input tokens only. Per Liquid’s pricing notes , images cost 1.5 tokens per 32×32-pixel patch. A 1024×1024 image therefore costs 1,536 tokens. Each question is billed as its own prompt, including its text and all images. So 3 questions on 1 image bill that image 3 times. The endpoint docs cap requests at 8 images and 10,000 image patches. The full JSON body must stay under 4.5 MB. Check out the official blog post , the decision model docs , and try the d1 Playground . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: Meta Releases Muse Spark Open: 816B Open-Weight MoE With 1M Context
abstract: Meta Superintelligence Labs has released Muse Spark Open , the open-weight version of its Muse Spark model. Muse Spark Open is an 816B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model that activates 42B parameters per token. It takes text, image, video and audio input, returns text, and holds a 1M-token context window. Meta team claims it to be the most capable US open-weight model to date. For developers, the real news is deployment: the NVFP4 build runs on 2 Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal MoE model from Meta, built for coding and long-horizon agentic work. Weights ship in BF16 and NVFP4 on Hugging Face. The open version received extra safety post-training. Meta team states that this makes it more robust without system-level guardrails. The model card lists 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each MoE layer holds 256 experts, and top-k routing activates 8 per token. Attention is grouped-query, with 128 query heads and 16 KV heads. A separate 1.8B-parameter Perception Encoder handles visual input. The vocabulary has 202,048 tokens, and training data covers more than 100 languages. Reasoning depth is set with reasoning_effort : low, medium, high or xhigh. The default is xhigh. Meta compares it with Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B and others at maximum reasoning effort. Its strongest results are on tool use and knowledge reliability: Coding is the weak spot. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the Terminus 2 harness, it scores 76.4. Kimi K3 reaches 85.0, GLM 5.3 scores 83.9 and Qwen3.8 scores 82.0. Its Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is 39. That sits behind GLM 5.3 (45), Kimi K3 (44) and Qwen3.8 (40). So “most capable US” holds, but Chinese open models still lead overall. Some rival scores are self-reported; the evaluation methodology lists each source. Per Meta’s developer guide , BF16 weights are about 1.6 TB. NVFP4 quantizes only the experts and lands near 530 GB. The model card recommends at least 700 GB of VRAM for NVFP4 and 2 TB for BF16. Day-one engines include SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth. Hosted APIs are live on Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. OpenRouter lists $1.25 per 1M input tokens and $4.25 per 1M output tokens. Two draft models speed up decoding: DFlash V2 for SGLang and DSpark for vLLM. Meta reports 3.7x single-request throughput with DFlash V2 on AMD MI355X. Fine-tuning works with TorchTitan, Hugging Face TRL and NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel. The Muse Model License permits use, fine-tuning, distillation and redistribution. 2 conditions matter most: Internal use, research and powering your own product features are exempt from the revenue clause. Check out the model weights , research blog , developer guide and evaluation methodology . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B Open Multimodal Agent Model
abstract: NVIDIA just released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL , an open vision-language model built for always-on enterprise agents. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts model from NVIDIA that activates 12B parameters per token. It reads text, images, documents and video, then reasons, calls tools and writes code in one model. For developers, 1 open checkpoint replaces a separate text model along with a separate vision model. NVIDIA also shipped 2 edge models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B and Bolt E4B. It is an open multimodal agent model. Weights ship under the OpenMDW-1.1 license . NVIDIA also released open datasets , training recipes and RL environments in NeMo Gym. The model card lists text, image and video inputs with text output. Video is limited to MP4 clips up to 2 minutes. Reasoning can be toggled on or off through the chat template. The backbone interleaves Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts and attention layers. Each MoE layer holds 512 routed experts. A C-RADIO vision encoder and a connector feed images, document pages and video frames into the language backbone. Speed comes from four techniques: The model was distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA team states that it trained on about 26 trillion tokens. Post-training used roughly 3.8 million samples plus RL across dozens of environments. Continued pretraining added 10B Indic tokens. title: Agentic RAG vs. Naive RAG: When Your Retrieval System Should Think for Itself
abstract: Agentic RAG vs. Naive RAG: When Your Retrieval System Should Think for Itself From static retrieval pipelines to autonomous reasoning engines: a complete breakdown of how these two architectures work, where each falls short, and how to choose the right one for your use case. By Vinod Chugani on October 16, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Large language models are remarkable text generators, but they have a well-documented weakness: they hallucinate. Without access to verified, up-to-date information, they confidently produce plausible-sounding answers that are factually wrong. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) emerged as the standard solution, grounding model outputs in external knowledge sources and dramatically reducing hallucinations across enterprise applications. But as organizations push these systems into more complex workflows, a new problem has surfaced. Standard RAG pipelines are linear — they retrieve once, pass those results to the model, and generate an answer. When the query is simple and the knowledge base is well-structured, this works fine. When the query requires multi-step reasoning, cross-referencing multiple sources, or synthesizing information that doesn't exist in a single document, the pipeline starts to crack. That's where Agentic RAG comes in. Rather than treating retrieval as a single, fixed step, it gives the system the ability to reason about how to search, evaluate what it finds, and iterate until it reaches a satisfying answer. We'll break down how both architectures work, look at where standard RAG hits its limits, and walk through the specific capabilities that make agentic systems better suited for complex tasks. By the end, you'll have a clear framework for deciding which approach fits your next project. The Baseline: Understanding Naive RAG Before examining where retrieval systems are going, it helps to be precise about where they started. Naive RAG — also called standard RAG — follows a rigid three-stage pipeline: Retrieve → Read → Generate . A user submits a query, the system converts it into a vector embedding, runs a similarity search against a vector database, retrieves the top-k most relevant document chunks, and passes those chunks to the large language model (LLM) as context. The model then generates a response based on what was retrieved. Think of it like a student preparing for an exam in a large library. Naive RAG is the student who types a single keyword into the catalog, grabs the first three books on the shelf, and writes an essay based only on what's in front of them — without stopping to check whether those sources actually answer the question. Under the hood, here's what happens. When documents are ingested, they're split into chunks and converted into dense vector representations using an embedding model. These vectors are stored in a database optimized for approximate nearest-neighbor search. At inference time, the user's query is embedded using the same model, and the database returns the chunks whose vectors are closest in high-dimensional space. Those chunks are then injected into the LLM's context window as a reference. This was a genuine breakthrough. Naive RAG made it possible to build enterprise Q&A systems, internal knowledge assistants, and document summarizers that stayed grounded in verified sources. For many applications, it remains an excellent and cost-effective choice. The Bottleneck: Where Naive RAG Breaks Down The architecture's core weakness is its linearity. A single retrieval pass either succeeds or it doesn't. If the initial query is poorly formed, if the relevant information is spread across multiple documents, or if the answer requires reasoning across several steps, the pipeline has no way to recover. The Single-Pass Limitation Naive RAG gets one shot at retrieval. If the query's embedding doesn't return the right chunks, the model is left generating a response from incomplete or irrelevant context. It can't recognize that the retrieval failed, and it can't try a different approach. Multi-Hop Reasoning Failures Consider a query like: "What regulatory policies does the company that acquired WhatsApp follow in the European Union?" Answering this correctly requires at least two steps: Identify that Meta acquired WhatsApp. Retrieve Meta's EU regulatory policies. A single vector search against "WhatsApp EU regulatory policies" will likely fail to bridge that connection — especially if those two pieces of information live in separate documents. Naive RAG has no way to decompose this into sequential sub-questions, retrieve the intermediate answer, and then use it to inform a second search. Susceptibility to Bad Retrieval When the top-k results are genuinely irrelevant to the query, the LLM faces an impossible situation. It either generates a response that ignores its grounding context (which produces hallucinations) or outputs an honest but unhelpful "I don't have enough information to answer." In high-stakes enterprise settings, neither outcome is acceptable. Agentic RAG: Giving the System a Brain Agentic RAG reframes the retrieval problem entirely. Instead of treating the LLM as a passive text generator that receives context and produces output, it treats the LLM as an autonomous reasoning engine that actively orchestrates the entire retrieval process. Where Naive RAG is a pipeline, Agentic RAG is a loop: Plan → Execute → Evaluate → Repeat . Back to the library analogy. A dedicated research assistant doesn't just grab the first three books and start writing. They read the initial sources, notice a key piece of evidence is missing, open a different database, cross-reference two conflicting claims, and only sit down to write once they're confident their sources are sufficient. Agentic RAG builds that behavior into the retrieval system itself. The LLM is no longer a consumer of retrieved context — it's the orchestrator, deciding what to retrieve, where to retrieve it from, whether the results are good enough, and what to do if they aren't. This transforms retrieval from a fixed pre-processing step into a dynamic, self-correcting process. The core shift: in Naive RAG, the model sees the retrieved context once. In Agentic RAG, the model reasons about the retrieval itself, deciding when to search, what to search for, and when it has enough information to generate a reliable answer. Four Mechanisms That Make RAG Agentic The difference between a naive and agentic pipeline isn't a single design choice — it's the accumulation of four distinct mechanisms, each addressing a specific failure mode that linear retrieval can't handle on its own. Query Routing Not all questions belong to the same data source. A financial analysis query might be best answered by querying a structured SQL database. A policy question might call for semantic search across unstructured documents. A request for current events might need a live web search. Query routing gives the system the ability to decide where to search before executing the search. The LLM examines the incoming query and selects the appropriate tool or data source from a predefined registry. This prevents the common failure mode of forcing every query through a single retrieval mechanism regardless of whether it fits. Query Decomposition Complex questions almost always contain multiple sub-questions, and an agentic system handles this by breaking the original prompt into smaller, independently answerable components before executing any retrieval at all. Back to the WhatsApp example: the system doesn't search for "WhatsApp EU regulatory policies" as a single phrase. Instead, it first asks which company acquired WhatsApp, retrieves that answer (Meta), and then uses that intermediate result to construct a second, more precise query about Meta's EU regulatory obligations. Each answer informs the next search, building toward a complete response through a chain of targeted retrievals rather than a single broad one.

title: 5 Best Resources to Learn About World Models in 2026
abstract: 5 Best Resources to Learn About World Models in 2026 World models could be the next big shift in AI. Learn more right now. By Kanwal Mehreen , KDnuggets Technical Editor & Content Specialist on October 16, 2026 in Language Models World models are becoming one of the most interesting areas of modern AI research. Instead of simply mapping an input to an output, a world model learns how an environment behaves . It can predict what might happen next, simulate possible outcomes, and help an AI system plan its actions. Although recent systems have brought world models into video generation, robotics, embodied AI, and physical reasoning, many of their fundamental ideas come from reinforcement learning and model-based planning. There is no single resource that takes you from the fundamentals all the way to systems such as Dreamer , Genie , and modern world foundation models, but we do have enough resources to understand how it all works. Here are the five best resources I found for learning about world models in 2026. 1. UC Berkeley CS 285: Deep Reinforcement Learning If you are completely new to world models, I would start here rather than jumping directly into recent world-model papers. UC Berkeley's CS 285: Deep Reinforcement Learning , taught by Sergey Levine, covers the foundations required to understand why world models are useful in the first place. The course covers reinforcement learning, control, and deep learning, and also includes dedicated material on model-based reinforcement learning. The most relevant parts are the lectures on planning, optimal control, learned dynamics, and model-based reinforcement learning. It has lecture recordings, notes, and assignments, so you can study both the mathematics and practical implementations. 2. Stanford CS348K: Introduction to World Models Once you understand some reinforcement learning, Stanford's Introduction to World Models lecture provides a much more direct entry into the topic. The lecture is part of Stanford's Spring 2026 CS348K course and is available online with downloadable PDF slides. It covers visual and spatial computing workloads including generative AI-based world creation, latent world representations, non-pixel-based approaches, and embodied agentic AI. It's not a full course, but it is a good starting point for understanding what world models actually are. 3. World Models by David Ha and Jurgen Schmidhuber This is probably the single most important resource for world models. The original World Models work by David Ha and Jürgen Schmidhuber popularized a simple but powerful idea: an agent can learn a compressed representation of its environment, learn how that representation evolves, and then train a controller using its internally simulated environment. The architecture consists of three main components. The vision model compresses observations into a smaller latent representation The memory model learns how those latent states change over time The controller uses this learned representation to decide which action to take The most interesting idea is that an agent can sometimes train inside its learned environment rather than interacting with the real environment for every training step. The project website is good for beginners — it includes explanations, diagrams, animations, experiments, and links to the implementation. Even though modern systems such as Dreamer and large video-based world models are more complex, the core intuition is very similar. 4. Stanford World Models and Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Reading List Once you understand the basic idea behind world models, the next step is figuring out what to read. There are now hundreds of papers related to learned dynamics, model-based reinforcement learning, latent environments, generative simulators, and embodied world models. This Stanford reading list provides a much more manageable starting point. It currently highlights ten important papers tracing the progression from early neural world models to modern approaches. The list includes World Models , PlaNet , Dreamer , DreamerV2 , SimPLe , DayDreamer , Genie , and TD-MPC2 . This sequence is useful because you can see how the field evolved. The original World Models showed that an agent could learn a compact internal simulator. PlaNet explored planning directly inside learned latent dynamics. Dreamer shifted toward learning policies using imagined trajectories. Later systems extended similar concepts into robotics and large-scale generative environments. Instead of randomly searching for papers on world models, you can simply work through this reading list one paper at a time. 5. Awesome World Model + Comprehensive World Models Survey Researchers associated with Tsinghua University created the Awesome World Model repository alongside their survey, Understanding World or Predicting Future? A Comprehensive Survey of World Models . The survey was accepted by ACM Computing Surveys , while the repository continuously organizes papers and resources across different branches of world-model research. It covers areas such as: Model-based reinforcement learning Self-supervised learning Large language and multimodal models Video generation and interactive 3D environments Game intelligence and embodied intelligence Autonomous driving and urban intelligence The accompanying survey is especially useful once you have learned the basics, because it explains how all these apparently different research directions fit under the broader world-model umbrella. I would not recommend reading the entire repository from top to bottom. Instead, bookmark it and use it as a reference whenever you want to explore a particular branch of the field. Bonus: World Models Handbook If you prefer learning from a book rather than jumping between lectures and research papers, Michael Brenndoerfer's World Models Handbook is one of the most relevant resources available. It can be read online for free, and a PDF version is also available for purchase. The book is still being completed: the site currently lists 72 planned chapters, with 39 published. It starts with a small end-to-end world model before introducing foundations such as dynamical systems, partial observability, Bayesian filtering, system identification, uncertainty, physics, and causality. Later sections move into modern architectures, including recurrent state-space models, transformers, autoregressive token models, diffusion and flow models, predictive embeddings such as JEPA, and multimodal foundation models . It also covers planning approaches and major research lines — Dreamer, MuZero, TD-MPC, Genie, Cosmos, and vision-language-action models. Wrapping Up World models are not one particular neural-network architecture. They lie at the intersection of reinforcement learning, representation learning, planning, video generation, robotics, control, and embodied AI , which makes them difficult to learn by simply opening the newest paper. A better strategy is to work backward from the fundamentals. First understand how an agent can learn and plan with a model of its environment. Then study the original neural world models architecture. After that, explore how newer research extends the same idea to latent representations, large-scale simulators, video prediction, robotics, and physical AI. Kanwal Mehreen is a machine learning engineer and a technical writer with a profound passion for data science and the intersection of AI with medicine. She co-authored the ebook "Maximizing Productivity with ChatGPT". As a Google Generation Scholar 2022 for APAC, she champions diversity and academic excellence. She's also recognized as a Teradata Diversity in Tech Scholar, Mitacs Globalink Research Scholar, and Harvard WeCode Scholar. Kanwal is an ardent advocate for change, having founded FEMCodes to empower women in STEM fields. <= Previous post

title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
abstract: Frontier Red Team Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins Oct 16, 2026 “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained. We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards. Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy. ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from. Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “ A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma ”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them . The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase: “I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.” Jerry Solinas, 2015 Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived. Claude found the seeds Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue. In under half an hour , Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp! The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp ( t ) for some number of iterations ( n ). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed. What this means This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure. How it was found Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state. Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48 , which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion. The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance. This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48 , with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own. However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock. Claude’s internal thinking at the time was: This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery. Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real. Claude found some base points too But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated? While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.

title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
abstract: Science Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude Oct 16, 2026 Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated. This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv . Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in qubits, which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as superposition —which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers. The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer. Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions. In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.) Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits. 1 These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classical algorithms , so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute. Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum circuits . These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run. We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2). In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components. Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper. These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner. Figure 1: Closed–loop quantum circuit optimization. Claude designs new implementations in Python, which are then sent to a programmatic evaluator. The evaluator checks whether the proposed implementation is correct, then scores it on the number of qubits and gates it requires. This information is then sent to Claude, which uses it to improve its implementation. The code and values shown are illustrative. Figure 2: Claude designed smaller and faster circuits across eight different quantum-circuit design tasks. Gray marks show the best previously published designs; orange marks and lines show Claude’s designs. Point addition, the eighth task, is compared in Table 1 below. A new reversible algorithm Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs. The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result.

title: How the Claude Code team does code review
abstract: We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it? This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent. We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year. Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible. Code review does two jobs: Find and fix issues before they ship Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end. We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily. Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second. So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it. THE LIFE OF A CHANGE A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.
