We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide . Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines. Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator." When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as: CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date. REVIEW.md , written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix. 2. AI review on every pull request Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else? On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code , is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.

title: How an Anthropic Japan BDR runs his day with a fleet of Claude agents
abstract: As a business development representative on Anthropic's Japan team, my job is to show Japanese companies how Claude can simplify and automate their workflows, but until earlier this year, most of mine were still manual. I was spending a couple of hours each morning routing and qualifying leads, then writing emails in Japanese or English. In the time I had left, I was updating our CRM, often a day or more behind. Now my agents prepare most of that before my day starts, and I review it. The first Claude-run workflow I built was pretty scrappy, but it did the job. I'd hand Claude one piece of my work at a time, correct what it got wrong, and save those corrections. Over time, that grew into a handful of agents, each covering a different routine. Word got around quickly, and teammates started asking for my prompts and skills so they could build their own. All I could send them was a zip file with my skills and a few Markdown files from the knowledge base, which they had to upload to Claude and then answer a round of setup questions before anything worked. My own setup was getting harder to keep track of, too. Each agent was a skill, a scheduled task and a shared folder, and I changed them by asking Claude in whatever chat I had open, so the same skill was being edited from lots of different conversations. I wanted to define each agent once, in one place, and be able to see every change I'd made to it. So I decided to try Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab) (beta), our managed agent infrastructure on the Claude Platform. I was hesitant to try it at first. The docs talk about schedules, tools, and credential vaults, and I'm a sales rep, so I assumed Managed Agents was for developers who can build and maintain the necessary infrastructure. I tried it anyway because my agents already existed, and I only had to move them over. It turned out I didn't need to be a developer. I described each agent's job in plain language, Claude wrote a few short setup scripts, and I ran them from the terminal on my laptop. (If you're starting from scratch, the Console also has a quickstart with ready-made agent templates.) Since then, there has been no infrastructure for me to look after. In this post, I'll walk through how I designed and prototyped the fleet, why I moved it to Managed Agents, how Claude Tag picks up anything that falls outside the routine, how it all changed my week, and what I'd tell sellers who want to build their own agents to automate manual, repetitive workflows. Designing my fleet of agents I divided up my workflow across several agents and gave every agent one clear job. A single responsibility keeps each one easy to reason about and easy to track, especially when something is off. I also gave every agent a Japanese name, because they mostly work in Japanese. Together they're called the Nakama , "the crew," or more literally, the companions you work with: Furiwake ("sorting") kicks off first: it reads the daily inbound queue and routes each lead to the right rep on the team, balancing the number of leads and the priority of each one and checking who's in that day, so every lead has an owner before any of us start our day. At the end of each run it posts a report to a dedicated Slack channel (every lead in, every lead assigned) so I can track the handoff. Sabaki ("handling") triages the leads that are assigned to me: it qualifies each lead, categorizes it against pre-set criteria, takes the defined next step for that category (draft a reply pointing them to to self-serve, craft a customized first email), updates the lead record in Salesforce, and drafts the first-touch email. It sources the draft's contents from the Nakama 's shared knowledge base, a memory store (opens in new tab) every agent reads and writes (more on this below). Henji ("reply") scans my inbox hourly for customer emails that need a response and prepares a draft reply in Japanese or English, depending on the thread, drawing on the same knowledge base as Sabaki . I can review, edit, and send the draft. Shoudan ("opportunity") reads recent customer interactions and pushes updates into Salesforce, so opportunity records stay current without manual data entry. Nokori ("what remains") runs at the end of the day: it scans my calendar, reads the attached meeting transcripts, summarizes each meeting, and drafts the follow-ups, again from the same knowledge base. Each agent runs on a schedule . A sixth agent, the Nakama's coordinator, is the fleet’s operations manager. It updates the agents’ instructions and the shared knowledge base between runs. When I want to change how an agent works, I write what I want in plain language in the Nakama’s Slack channel. Only I can post requests for changes to agents’ instructions and system prompts. The coordinator checks that channel every 15 minutes or so, picks up the request, and makes the update. Prototyping the fleet in Claude You don't need Managed Agents to start. I prototyped the whole fleet in Claude first, using the following pieces: A skill per agent: the instructions for one job. A scheduled task for each skill, so I don’t need to run it manually. A shared folder on my laptop as the knowledge base every skill writes its learnings back into: the difference between what it drafted and what I sent, plus anything new it dug up along the way. On Managed Agents, the skill became the agent's system prompt, the scheduled task became a schedule on the agent's deployment (opens in new tab) , and the shared folder became a memory store. I still ask for changes in plain language, but now I do it all in one Slack channel, and each change to an agent's instructions is saved as a new version, so each agent keeps a numbered history of its instructions. I'd suggest starting in Claude and moving your agents to Managed Agents once you have more than you can comfortably keep track of. Running the fleet on Claude Managed Agents Three things I got on Managed Agents that mattered most for my workflow: The agents can run in the background The agents run on their schedule whether my laptop is open or not, even when it's offline. The schedule is part of each agent's deployment. I could schedule skills in Claude too, but each of those schedules was a task set up in my own app. On Managed Agents, I set the cadence and timezone in the Console, next to the deployed agent's instructions and tools, and I have no cron jobs to maintain on the side. If a run goes wrong, I can open it in the Console and see each step the agent took. And while I'm trying out a change to an agent, the scheduled runs keep using the version that’s deployed, so a half-finished edit doesn't end up in tomorrow's run. The Nakama shares one memory and learns from my edits Every agent reads and writes the same memory store (opens in new tab) , so any agent can use the others’ learnings. The agents compare the drafts they wrote with the emails I sent, and they save each difference as a note on how I'd phrase it. They also keep whatever new information they dig up while researching an answer, from our internal docs and our official websites. I fix a phrasing once in Henji's drafts, and Sabaki and Nokori stop making the same mistake. Credentials live in a managed vault with scoped permissions My agents have access to my email and our Salesforce records, but since these are customer conversations and company records, I wanted that access under control. The credentials live in managed vaults (opens in new tab) , which protect credentials agents use to log in to outside services, such as OAuth access and refresh tokens, API keys, and personal access tokens. Each agent’s deployment uses only the vaults its job needs, it never sees the credentials, and I can revoke access in one step. Handing the next steps to Claude Tag For most of what the Nakama produces, I only need to read a draft in my inbox and send it, or glance at an updated Salesforce record.

title: Code Review is now generally available
abstract: Code Review is out of research preview and available to Claude Team and Enterprise organizations. Eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Code Review credits by January 15, 2027. Credits expire 30 days after you claim them. Terms apply. What's new in Code Review Coding agents keep increasing the pace at which teams write code, and the review bottleneck hasn't eased. For general availability, we made Code Review faster, better at finding the bugs that matter, and easier to tune to each of your repositories. Since we released the research preview , Code Review has gotten sharper, catching more of the bugs that would otherwise reach production. We also run Code Review on pull requests at Anthropic, which shows us where reviews slow our own engineers down. Teams using Code Review during the preview told us the rest: it was catching real issues before a human reviewer looked at the PR, but they wanted reviews that were quieter, sized to each change, and faster. Here’s what we shipped: Speed: Most reviews now finish about 3x faster (~20 minutes down to 6-10 minutes) compared to during preview. Quality: Find more of the bugs that matter, with clear, concise findings that state the problem, what triggers it, and the fix in a few sentences. Flexibility: Admins choose Quick, Standard (default), or Deep for each repository, so routine codebases get a quick pass and the most critical ones get a deep review. Every level delivers high-quality reviews. Get started Code Review is now generally available for Team and Enterprise plans. For admins : Enable Code Review in your Claude Code settings , install the GitHub App, and select repositories you’d like to run reviews on. For developers : Once enabled, reviews run automatically on new PRs. No configuration needed. Explore the docs for more information.

title: Code, Test, and Deploy on One Machine with NVIDIA RTX Spark
abstract: AI agents are changing how software gets built. Developers have gone from writing every line of code by hand to directing agents that write most of the code. As a result, the current workflow is split across a laptop, a cloud model API, and a cloud VM. NVIDIA RTX Spark is built for AI development. Thanks to the NVIDIA GB10 system-on-a-chip and large unified memory, developers can run local coding agents, access AI frameworks, and code, test, and deploy on a single PC. One machine to code, test, and deploy RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops enable developers to complete all of their workflow on a single machine. Developers can choose to work in Windows, including the new Windows Developer Config, developed with Microsoft, which installs the top development frameworks, mutes notifications, enhances the terminal, and can move their task bar to the side. Or they can work in Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they get access to the same environment and dependencies they will use when deploying to the cloud. This enables developers to complete all their work in their target OS without code migrations. And since RTX Spark has an NVIDIA GPU, developers can test and deploy to the largest local AI installed base: 150 million RTX PCs, as well as virtually all the clouds in the world that run on NVIDIA GPUs. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI compute, developers can run coding models locally, including Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, reducing cloud coding agent token consumption. The performance you need for AI development Development has gone from being a CPU-bound workload, where performance was determined mostly by the CPU, to a GPU-bound workload. AI developers today need to run inference to run their coding agents and test their apps; for fine-tuning and training models; and yes, still a bit of compilation. Thanks to the NVIDIA Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU in RTX Spark, these laptops and desktops come equipped with all the compute required for inference, fine-tuning and compilation. Compared with Intel’s Panther Lake 12Xe, RTX Spark delivers 4.6x performance on coding agents, 2.7x performance on fine-tuning, and 1.8x performance on code compilation. Figure 1. NVIDIA developer-workload comparison, with Intel Core Ultra X9 388H normalized to 1.0. Tests: AA-AgentPerf-local with Qwen3.8-27B; Unsloth LoRA with Llama-3.1-8B; and Linux kernel compilation using Phoronix Test Suite A familiar software stack, expanded for Windows NVIDIA partnered with Microsoft to advance the Windows on Arm developer landscape. Together with RTX Spark, the community is releasing multiple new tools, including the first PyTorch-CUDA build, the first Python release that is native by default with Python 3.15, over 2,000 ready-to-use Conda packages, and Arm-compatible versions for more than 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages. A key advantage of developing on NVIDIA hardware is access to the largest ecosystem of developer tools, from coding agents, to AI models, to frameworks. Because NVIDIA GPUs are the most widely used platform for AI development, new tools and frameworks typically work on NVIDIA from day one, while support for other hardware follows weeks later. There’s also access to NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including tools such as FlashInfer for LLM acceleration and NVIDIA NeMo libraries tools for AI model development. NVIDIA also provides a repository of NVIDIA Skills that teach agents how to use CUDA-X libraries, enabling developers to build GPU-accelerated applications without requiring deep familiarity with CUDA. Figure 2. RTX Spark’s ecosystem of agents, models, frameworks, and CUDA-X libraries Local coding agents come to RTX Spark RTX Spark devices are ideal for local coding agents. NVIDIA has collaborated closely with the top agents, including GitHub Copilot, Pi, Hermes, and OpenClaw, to improve them and make them easier to use. The improvements include: Seamless deployment of local models with optimized recipes Enhanced security with NVIDIA OpenShell and/or Microsoft Execution Containers, delivering OS-level sandboxing Hybrid prompt routers between local and cloud models, so that prompts get sent to local models if they are good enough, or escalated to cloud if needed, reducing token consumption Microsoft GitHub CoPilot now enables seamless local AI through Windows ML, which is now supported with llama.cpp as a backend. The prompt router HydraFusion has been upgraded to also support local models. And the new MAI 1.1 Coding Flash model can run locally on RTX Spark. Pi , an open-source coding agent with a lightweight terminal interface and support for local and cloud models, is also optimized for RTX Spark. Its extensions, skills, and prompt templates give developers control over how the agent fits into their workflow, from model selection to the tools it can use. JetBrains has launched native support for Junie Local on RTX Spark . The coding agent reads code, edits files, and runs tests, with the model and code staying on the machine. Junie Local sizes its context window to the memory available to the GPU, so RTX Spark unified memory lets it keep more code, tool output, and conversation history in context. New Nemotron models offer more options for local agents Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint. Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source, including training data, weights and recipes, so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents. Decision models now supported in top frameworks Decision models are the latest breakthrough in AI development. They give AI agents a near-instant way to make decisions, without lengthy reasoning loops. They can choose what to do next, from classifying requests, to selecting the next action, up to 200x faster than traditional agents. Decision models are now supported in llama.cpp and Unsloth on RTX Spark and GeForce RTX GPUs. AI for media SDKs The NVIDIA AI for Media SDKs are now available for RTX Spark, including Python wheel with support for video super resolution, frame generation, and TrueHDR. The wheel is available on PyPI, with C++ SDKs also available on NGC for RTX Spark and Windows on Arm. Bring your Windows applications to RTX Spark To bring an existing application to RTX Spark, first assess dependencies for Windows on Arm. Choose a native Arm64 build or use Arm64EC to migrate components incrementally. Test installation, functionality, performance, and the NVIDIA and CUDA paths your app uses. NVIDIA’s app-porting resources explain the migration options and tools, including how to start preparation on an existing Windows on Arm development system. Find your RTX Spark and start building RTX Spark is available now in laptops, and coming in November to small form factor desktops that are ideal for always on, 24×7 running agents. Explore RTX Spark systems to find your favorite and see available purchasing options. Once you get your own, get started with the AI Development playbook to configure Windows, set up your agent, and connect NVIDIA Skills. And learn about how you can get started developing Local AI apps for NVIDIA GPUs.

title: Introducing Reflection Beam: an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS
abstract: Reflection AI introduced Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks such as maintaining code, using tools, interpreting results, and completing multi-step workflows. The open-weight release gives developers and researchers control over the runtime, deployment environment, and customization process. In this post, we explain Reflection’s vision and show how you can deploy Beam on AWS. Start with an Amazon SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint for a fully managed path. When you need Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure, use Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM. We also explain how Beam’s 501 billion total parameters shape checkpoint storage, weight memory, sharding, and parallelism, while its 23 billion active parameters influence per-token compute. At launch, Beam is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). Reflection’s mission is to make intelligence open and accessible to all through open model weights, published research, and open source software. Its full AI stack spans models, core software, production infrastructure, and applications. Beam brings this approach to developers building software engineering and agentic systems. Beam is a sparse mixture-of-experts model for resolving software issues, modifying code, calling tools, and acting on intermediate results. It has 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active parameters, and Reflection reports an effective context length of 1 million tokens. Reflection releases Beam’s weights through Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam 1.0 is available in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoint variants. These formats provide different memory footprints and hardware compatibility. You can deploy the model with the AWS managed JumpStart container configuration or inspect and customize the model with SGLang or vLLM in your AWS environment. Choose the serving path that meets your control and scaling requirements. The JumpStart real-time path packages the model, container, and endpoint behind a managed deployment workflow. The HyperPod path exposes the cluster and serving runtime so that you can control distributed execution, caching, routing, and scaling. title: Closing the Binary Blind Spot: Domain-Knowledge Injection for LLM Malware Triage in npm Packages
abstract: Supply chain attacks on package registries have grown in volume and sophistication [1]. Public research regularly observes malware being deployed to the npm registry by a range of threat actors, from spam campaigns [2] to the steady proliferation of DPRK malware [3, 4, 5], and to the high-impact TeamPCP in 2025 and 2026 [6, 7], with the DPRK and TeamPCP actors having a track record of successfully compromising widely used open source projects for maximized downstream reach [8]. To study this problem directly, we have been collecting npm malware samples since November 2025, and observed that, among the 11,413 package-versions we scanned and corroborated through OSV npm malware advisories [9], most malware on the npm registry hides its payload in the package source or fetches it from an external server, accounting for 96.2% of the corroborated dataset. The remaining 3.8%, 432 package-versions, bundle a binary. Though small in volume, they can carry disproportionate risk during triage. A stripped, opaque binary that carries no source for tools to read can be nested within a facade of clean source and metadata and potentially skew an LLM towards a benign verdict. We evaluate how a panel of LLMs reason over crafted binary payloads at varying obfuscation and ambiguity, identify the failure modes specific to this vector, and close them with a purpose-built, cost-effective encoding of domain knowledge that improves detection quality for both budget and frontier models alike. To support the wider research community, we built a scanner that monitors the npm registry in real time and runs a static stage before LLM triage, with YARA [10] on the tarball, Semgrep [11] and the npm registry API on the JavaScript and metadata, and a binary-analysis module over the compiled artifact. It assembles the output into a structured prompt, and the LLM returns a verdict with reasoning, requesting additional files over up to three rounds. Our analysis found packages with bundled binaries to be both the rarest and the hardest for the pipeline to triage. An adversary distributing malicious JavaScript can assume the target already has the runtime to execute the payload, whereas a binary must be compiled for a range of target machines. Across OSV-confirmed npm malware, binary-bearing packages fail to reach a decisive malicious verdict more than twice as often as source-only ones (14.4% vs 6.2%). Prior work instruction-tunes open-source models on expert-authored data, baking the knowledge into the weights [12]. That route cannot reach the closed, hosted models, and it requires retraining as the threat landscape shifts. We take the opposite approach and supply the expertise at inference, as pre-computed static evidence placed in the prompt before the model reasons. We evaluate whether LLMs can detect malicious logic concealed within precompiled binaries in otherwise clean packages. A secondary question is whether the detection failures are systematic rather than random. Third, whether encoding domain knowledge of the binary problem can improve detection accuracy. We built five payload types (Table 1) of native Node.js addons (.node files) covering common supply chain attack patterns. Imports range from defensible (fopen, connect, gethostname) to rarely legitimate (execve with dup2), and each package wraps the binary in a professional package.json, README, JavaScript bindings, and binding.gyp. The sysmon stealer spans an obfuscation ladder from a readable baseline to a hardened build with symbols stripped and strings XOR-encoded, while the other four types appear at a single obfuscation level. We chose single-byte XOR deliberately, since unlike a stronger cipher such as RC4 it leaves no structural markers in disassembly for a model to catch. The set mirrors collected malware. Across the OSV-confirmed npm packages shipping a binary, formats are PE, ELF (all stripped), and Mach-O, with behaviors spanning credential and environment theft, persistence, exfiltration and C2, host reconnaissance, and droppers. Table 1. Adversarial payload types and their import profiles. We evaluated nine models across seven providers (Table 2): seven budget models a team would realistically run across its codebase, four of them open-weight, and two higher-capability baselines as behavioral baseline references at higher price points. We also ran Claude Opus 4.6, the most expensive model, only as a cost reference. Table 2. Models evaluated and their roles. To isolate the profiles, each payload was scanned twice per model, once without profiles and once with them. Prompt, context, and binary analysis were identical across both runs. Inference settings were held constant across every model and both conditions: temperature 0, the same system and analysis prompts throughout, and an 8192-token output cap. A capability profile is a declarative playbook that encodes one malicious technique, such as credential harvesting or persistence, as a set of weighted conditions over the scanner's static evidence. The profiles cover source and binary techniques across npm and PyPI. Figure 1 shows how a profile enters a scan: Figure 1. The scan pipeline with capability profiles. Each model was scanned against all ten payloads. We count HIGHLY_SUSPICIOUS or MALICIOUS as a detection success; SUSPICIOUS or BENIGN on a known-malicious payload is a failure. The failure analysis centers on the seven-model budget tier (70 model-payload tests); the two baselines (20 tests) serve only as a reference ceiling and are reported separately. Without profiles, the budget tier failed on 35 of 70 tests (50%), 20 of them outright benign, and fell short of the malicious bar on 51 (73%). The two behavior baselines failed none at the escalation threshold and fell short of malicious only once (Sonnet, sysmon v3). Within the budget tier the failures followed distinct, repeatable model-specific patterns (Table 3) rather than random error; Gemini alone matched the baselines on detection, though through confabulated reasoning rather than genuine analysis. The full verdict and confidence matrix is in the appendix (Table A1). With profiles enabled, 32 of the 35 no-profile detection failures (91%) recover to a detection, and no model returns a benign verdict on any payload. Every model that failed without profiles reached full detection with them, except GPT-5.4-nano, whose three residual failures stay at suspicious on three payloads. Across the affordable tier, failures at the escalation threshold fell from 50% to 4% (3 of 70), and at the malicious bar from 73% to 34%. Table 3. Per-model detection rate (verdict at highly suspicious or above on a known-malicious payload) without and with capability profiles. The clearest single case is Qwen3-Next on the obfuscated sysmon-native stealer: benign at 0.98 recommending allowlist without profiles, malicious at 0.98 recommending block with them, on byte-identical input, after four profiles fired. The baselines, Sonnet and Kimi, were already correct without profiles, and the evidence strengthens their verdicts, so the profiles reinforce rather than distort a model that already reasons correctly. Technique-specific profiles fired according to each payload’s attack pattern. Table 4. Capability profiles triggered per payload at critical or malicious threshold. The experiment surfaced four failure modes, each spanning a large fraction of the panel rather than any single model (Table 5). They are not mutually exclusive, since one benign verdict can be both a dismissal and a rationalization, so the table reports per-mode prevalence and a model's row can sum past ten. We read dismissal and hedging from the verdict tier, rationalization and confabulation from the written reasoning. Two factors explain them. The first is domain knowledge, which budget LLMs lack for interpreting binary structural evidence in a package's context [13]. The second is raw capability.

title: How our AI Research team uses AI Runtime
abstract: At Databricks, we continuously develop and evaluate new AI research techniques to make our products more intelligent, efficient, and useful for customers. Our research spans products like Genie, Smart Routing, and AI Functions. Recently, we've published how we made search 3x faster , developed new techniques for offline reinforcement learning , and pushed the frontier of complex document extraction . To build great AI models and manage hundreds of parallel research workstreams, we need infrastructure that can keep pace. That's why we use Databricks AI Runtime (AIR). In this post, we'll share how AIR helps us experiment quickly, scale to large training workloads, and adapt to agent-led training, along with what we've learned about managing GPU resources across research projects. Our research team develops models that power Databricks AI Functions , including ai_parse_document and ai_extract . For example, Databricks AI Functions deliver state-of-the-art document parsing quality , backed by models trained to understand enterprise documents. Achieving that quality requires extensive research across different architectures, datasets, training techniques, and hyperparameters, spanning tens of thousands of training and evaluation runs. We use supervised fine-tuning (SFT), offline reinforcement learning (RL), and online RL to train models ranging from a few billion parameters to nearly a trillion. Depending on the workload, we use NVIDIA H100 or B300 GPUs, both available through AIR. Our largest training runs can require hundreds of GPUs working together over days or weeks, with high-bandwidth networking to keep training efficient. Supporting these workloads creates three challenges: Our research team has been customer zero of AI Runtime since the product's inception last year. We use AIR to develop, train, and test models that power Databricks AI products, relying on its GPU infrastructure and integration with our existing tools. AIR performs preflight checks on assigned GPU nodes to ensure they're healthy and can communicate effectively before training starts. It also monitors node health during execution, detecting issues such as NCCL communication failures, thermal or power throttling, and GPU driver problems. If a node becomes unhealthy and causes a job to fail, AIR detects the issue and cordons off the affected node so subsequent jobs aren't scheduled on the same problematic infrastructure. This is especially important for projects like KARL, where complex rollout generation and post-training of models with more than 100 billion parameters can require thousands of GPU hours. Rather than repeatedly troubleshooting infrastructure failures, we can focus on improving our models. Fast iteration with the AIR CLI and custom containers Research requires us to change model configurations, training approaches, and code frequently. With the AIR CLI, we can launch workloads programmatically, specify the GPUs we need, and let AIR handle provisioning and scheduling, including high-bandwidth networking for distributed training across clouds. We also rely on custom Docker containers for local development. AIR lets us use those same images for training, ensuring compatibility without recreating our environments. We can upload our codebase, execute custom code in those containers, and use Databricks Artifact Registry to register and share images across experiments. AIR's investments in launch latency and container optimization help us start training jobs in seconds, shortening feedback loops as we test new ideas. MLflow and logging for experiment tracking We use MLflow to track our research experiments. AIR automatically creates and manages MLflow experiments for our training jobs, eliminating separate configuration. We can monitor job status, stream and inspect training logs, and retrieve metrics to understand how experiments are progressing. This also gives our AI agents access to the information they need to evaluate results and determine what to try next. Seamless, governed access to research data All of our research data is stored in Unity Catalog. Through Unity Catalog FUSE mounting, AIR lets us access that data as though it were part of a local filesystem, even when working across different Databricks workspaces. This keeps our data accessible, tracked, shareable, and governed without changing how our training code interacts with files. Combined with MLflow and our Docker-based environments, it gives us a consistent workflow from local development to distributed training. Managing GPU capacity across research projects Our workloads have very different resource needs. A debugging experiment may require only a few GPUs, while a large training run might need hundreds for days or weeks. Different projects also have competing timelines and priorities. AIR's workload prioritization and preemption capabilities help us allocate resources across projects, prioritize time-sensitive experiments, and use excess capacity when it's available. For example, spare capacity can support additional exploratory experiments over a weekend without disrupting higher-priority work. Our goal is to keep GPU resources available for the experiments that matter, without requiring researchers to manually coordinate infrastructure. Popularized by Andrej Karpathy, autoresearch is changing how we develop AI models. Instead of researchers manually launching and evaluating every experiment, we're increasingly using agents to propose changes, run experiments, evaluate results, and determine what to try next. This shift has dramatically increased our experimentation volume. Across our AI Functions research workloads, the number of training jobs has grown by 8x . As agents take on more of the research process, our infrastructure needs to keep up. A slow startup or confusing configuration error might be manageable when a researcher launches a handful of experiments. When agents launch hundreds, those same issues quickly become bottlenecks. Agent-driven research requires fast job launches, programmatic interfaces, clear and actionable errors, reliable execution, and accessible training results. Our autoresearch workflow follows a continuous cycle: AIR is particularly well suited to this workflow because agents can interact with it programmatically and benefit from its fast job launches, built-in reliability, and ability to scale. Through the Databricks CLI and databricks-air-skills , our agents can launch concurrent workloads, monitor job status, retrieve MLflow metrics, and iterate based on the results. This lets us run more experiments while our researchers focus on developing new ideas and improving model quality. As we move further toward agent-driven research, AIR gives us the infrastructure to support both larger models and a faster pace of experimentation. Our experience using AI Runtime has shown us how much reliable, flexible GPU infrastructure matters for research. From large-scale training and governed data access to agent-driven experimentation, AIR lets us spend less time managing infrastructure and more time developing better models. If you're training or fine-tuning your own models, check out the AI Runtime documentation to get started. AI Runtime has also powered our research across areas like faster search , reinforcement learning , and document understanding . title: Stripe Data Pipeline now syncs real-time Stripe data to Lakebase Postgres
abstract: If your business runs on Stripe, your application needs access to Stripe data at runtime to respond to customer activity, whether that's confirming a payment, updating subscription access, or displaying billing details. Keeping that data in sync with Stripe has traditionally meant building and maintaining custom integrations with APIs or webhooks. That's changing. Stripe Data Pipeline now supports real-time sync to Postgres [link Stripe's blog post], and Databricks Lakebase is one of the supported destinations ( blog and documentation ) powered by OpenSharing. Stripe streams real-time API data into Lakebase and manages the sync end to end. Earlier this year, Stripe data became available to sync to Databricks through Stripe Data Pipeline. With real-time sync to Postgres, one Stripe account can now feed two Databricks destinations, each built for a different kind of work. Stripe shares your payments, customers, subscriptions, refunds, and payouts data with your workspace through Delta Sharing , so your Stripe data becomes just another table in Unity Catalog , governed and ready to join with the rest of your business data. Teams use it to score which customers are likely to churn, ask Genie for MRR by geography, reconcile payments at month-end, and give finance teams governed apps to explore payment data. These workloads look at patterns across thousands of customers and many weeks of history. With Stripe Data Pipeline's real-time sync to Postgres , your payment, customer, subscription, and other Stripe data is continuously synced to Lakebase, with updates arriving within seconds. Your application can query this data to drive its logic, determining what actions to take and what content to surface based on an up-to-date view of Stripe data. Keeping your application's database up to date with real-time Stripe data takes ongoing effort. Today, most teams rely on one of two approaches: Either way, it's a separate piece of infrastructure to build, monitor, and maintain. And when it fails, customers end up with the wrong access or outdated account details. That infrastructure work goes away with Stripe Data Pipeline. Choose which Stripe tables to sync to Lakebase, and Stripe handles the backfill, ongoing delivery, and data audits through its no-code pipeline, helping keep your data complete and up to date. With real-time Stripe data in Lakebase, your application can access the latest payment and subscription information to support core product functionality and customer experiences, including: When a customer upgrades their plan, their new subscription details are reflected in Lakebase within seconds, and your application unlocks premium features on their next request. When a subscription is canceled or a renewal fails, access changes just as quickly, with no event handler in between and no window where a paying customer is stuck on the free plan. Customers expect their account page to reflect what just happened: the plan they're on, the invoice that was paid this morning, the card that needs updating. With subscriptions, invoices, and payment data synced to Lakebase, your application can show accurate billing details wherever customers manage their account, without calling the Stripe API on every page load. With charges, refunds, and payouts syncing continuously, you can build dashboards that show daily sales volume, payouts, and refunds as they happen. With subscription and payment history right in your application database, you can serve contextual offers at the right moment: a win-back discount shortly after a customer cancels, an upgrade prompt when usage outgrows their plan, or a reminder when a payment method is about to expire. Real-time sync to Postgres for Stripe Data Pipeline is available in public preview, and it's free to get started. Create a pipeline in the Stripe Dashboard and read the documentation to learn more. Lakebase is Databricks' serverless Postgres database, built for applications and AI agents and integrated with the rest of the Databricks Data + AI Platform. Get started for free. title: Reducing the noise: How Atlassian built an OCSF security lakehouse on Databricks
abstract: Atlassian is a global SaaS provider serving 350,000 customers — the product of 20 years of growth and a long list of acquisitions, each of which arrived with its own logging formats. The result was a security data pipeline absorbing 44 billion events per day with no common language across various log sources. "You've got varied timestamps, you've got proprietary schemas, you've got operational drain for anyone trying to organize and structure this information," explained Zachary Schmerber, Senior Security Logging Engineer at Atlassian and a maintainer of the OCSF schema. Analysts were burning time normalizing data after it landed, cross-platform correlation was limited because data lived in different places and shapes, and SIEM pipelines were not keeping pace. The team needed a way to coalesce fragmented telemetry into one place and make sense of it, while maintaining flexibility and avoiding vendor lock-in. Atlassian's answer was to standardize everything on the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and build the lakehouse on Databricks. OCSF won because it was the only option the team considered wholly open . Compared to alternatives like ECS or UDM, it offered a strongly typed schema with robust validation that minimized ambiguity after transformation, good compression efficiency, extensibility, and an open-source community (with Linux Foundation backing and a path toward international standardization). Its roughly 40,000 fields looked daunting at first — but that verbosity turned out to be the platform's greatest asset, because the semantic context stays with the data. "Investigations where a single query could hit many different data sources — because the data is structured," said Schmerber. "Maybe you've got five vulnerability scanners in your system. Now you have one data set instead of five." Databricks was the natural platform. Native ACID transactions made it far easier to migrate across schema versions without breaking downstream consumers; auto-scaling Spark clusters handled shared, high-volume workloads; and the platform was built to manage the infrastructure overhead of a large, multi-team organization. Atlassian deliberately chose ETL over ELT — transforming data in flight — to enable real-time detection, preserve vendor independence, and compress data as it moved through the pipeline. Table optimization delivered dramatic performance gains. With structured OCSF data, partitioning and Z-ORDER took a representative query from ~45 seconds to 2–3 seconds — a 95% improvement , with similar gains on larger queries. Enabling Graviton clusters with Photon cut query cost and runtime by roughly two-thirds. A defining engineering decision was embedding the entire OCSF schema into Go structs — what the team calls "TypeGo." Because the schema lives in the type system, correctness is guaranteed at compile time. "Every time you produce a new OCSF log, it's pre-validated — because it can't be anything but OCSF," said Schmerber. Nested objects are native, deployments can run anywhere, and everything is unit tested. Crucially, this type safety also tamed AI: when the team automated transformation with an agentic workflow, the rigid schema sharply reduced hallucinations and cut token usage, because the agent couldn't produce invalid mappings and cycle through bad iterations. The biggest transformation was operational. Atlassian's security data-engineering team started with a six-phase manual procedure to collect logs, transform them into TypeGo, route, test, configure, and ship them via PR. Over time they automated nearly all of it — and eventually handed it back to the customer as a self-service platform. Now an analyst identifies the logs they want and provides a canonical dataset. After a gated confirmation, the workflow scans the framework inside the Go structs, generates the mappings and the DAG, tests them locally, deploys a canary configuration via PR, validates at scale in a canary environment, and — after a soak — gets promoted to production and notifies the user of any errors. Regression testing gates everything before production. The tool chain includes a schema-mapping IDE and an open-source Go OCSF library with validation performance enhancements, automatic handling of unmapped fields, schema helpers (IP path, normalization), and intelligent routing. The payoff is low onboarding overhead: "I can now have a SOC analyst do principal data engineer work in a production environment," said Schmerber — with every change still reviewed. The acceleration is stark: "It took me a year to map about one-third of the data we have mapped today," Schmerber noted, "and two months to map the other two-thirds." For the detection and response team, standardization changed how alerts get written. "Adopting the OCSF schema has enabled us to transform our threat detection pipeline by moving from one-to-one alerts to a signal- and risk-based detection methodology, where multiple signal findings are clustered together in a single alert," said Jordan of Atlassian's Detection and Response team. Using a custom tool called Alert Explorer , findings cluster around standardized OCSF values — for example, a single actor.user value that is identical whether it appears in an authentication event or a network event. That consistency lets the team standardize clustering, enrichment, and triage plays: instead of per-detection enrichment, they call an enrichment API on a standardized username value every time. "OCSF has made it much easier to write detections and provide more meaningful, actionable alerts," said Jordan, "which analysts can dive deep into regardless of where the data came from." Beyond the headline cost and performance numbers, standardization unlocked capabilities that were previously impractical: multi-domain correlation with strong entity resolution, efficient user-behavior analytics, and cross-application pattern analysis. With everything speaking one language, the team could write simple queries to spot anomalous behavior across five different routers — or five vulnerability scanners — at once. Dashboards were simplified dramatically because OCSF classes share objects, and storage was optimized because the team knew what data to keep and what to drop. Schmerber is most excited about what the semantically rich schema unlocks for AI. "How do you talk to your data unless your agent has context? It'll hallucinate and give you the wrong answer," he said. Because OCSF carries its definitions inside the schema, agentic assistance becomes far more accurate. The roadmap includes skills training that feeds an analyst's real field usage into reusable agent skills, an orchestration of agents that can run threat hunts with the right context, contextual SQL that can answer questions like "where's my DNS C2 traffic in this schema?", and context graphs built on OCSF. The longer-term ambition is semantic: making OCSF the canonical starting point that everything emits — rather than a model coalesced from data after the fact. The team will also continue with improving query performance by looking at a move to Liquid Clustering for data partitioning across environments like corporate devices and cloud. title: Geospatial queries are up to 38X faster with Lakehouse//RT
abstract: Spatial SQL and spatial joins now run on Lakehouse//RT and they're up to 38X faster than traditional cloud data warehouses. Earlier this year, we brought Spatial SQL to General Availability on Databricks: this included support for the GEOMETRY data type, 100+ spatial functions, high-performance spatial joins, AI/BI maps, Delta Sharing. The GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY data types are part of the open lakehouse, available in Apache Spark, and supported in the same underlying parquet files used by Delta and Iceberg v3. Customers across insurance, agriculture, energy, telecom, retail, logistics and more have adopted it to consolidate geospatial workloads onto a single governed platform. Organizations with both spatial OLAP workloads and real-time location-based applications want great performance and high concurrency. Many of these organizations still rely on traditional data warehouses and build out specialized architectures for spatial applications, sometimes managing a separate stack centered on PostGIS for every use case just to meet latency requirements. Separate stacks lead to more copies of data, more synchronization pipelines, and more governance overhead. Databricks now supports 4-pillars for geospatial workloads: Lakehouse for long-running spatial OLAP workloads, Lakebase for spatial OLTP, apps, and agents, Databricks Apps for purpose-built experiences, and now the Lakehouse//RT warehouse for real-time analytics. This blog covers what Lakehouse//RT delivers for spatial workloads, driving up to 38X performance improvement under high concurrency. We benchmarked Lakehouse//RT against a traditional cloud data warehouse across a suite of spatial queries using SpatialBench . By comparison, Lakehouse//RT delivers 3X faster on average, and up to 20X faster across the tested queries. Under heavy load, the performance differences are even more significant. At 50 concurrent users, Lakehouse//RT delivers up to 38X on the queries where the traditional warehouse could keep up. Try it for yourself: Follow the SpatialBench documentation to generate the synthetic data used in the benchmark queries from this page . Take a look at query #8. To follow best practices, it is recommended to remove the ST_GeomFromWKB call that converts data stored as well-known binary and instead use the native GEOMETRY data types. Using the native data types allows query optimizations and file-skipping to provide the best performance. Spatial SQL on Databricks already serves a wide range of industries. With Lakehouse//RT, workloads can run with the real-time speed applications demand. Here are a few examples: Spatial SQL on Lakehouse//RT is available now in Beta. To get started: At Data + AI Summit 2026, we introduced Lakehouse//RT , Databricks' new real-time data warehouse built to deliver millisecond query performance at massive concurrency directly on your lakehouse data . Lakehouse//RT was designed to solve a specific problem: as organizations expand data access across users, applications, dashboards, and AI agents, they need real-time responsiveness without copying data into a separate serving layer. Preview customers have seen significantly better performance overall with Lakehouse//RT vs. real-time serving layers, with latency as low as 10ms and concurrency as high as 12,000 queries per second. Yes. Spatial SQL and spatial joins now run on the Lakehouse//RT, so you can serve geospatial queries with low latency and high concurrency directly on your governed Delta and Iceberg tables.
